tutorials.title: Five ways your quick site gets hacked
tutorials.summary: You built a site in a weekend. The five doors that get opened most, how to test your own site for each in a minute, and how to close them.

steps.title: Everything you send is theirs now
steps.body: Whatever your site sends to a visitor **lives in their browser**, and it is not coming back.

steps.title: They can read it, change it, repeat it
steps.body: They can read every line, change any value, and **send the same request a thousand times**.

steps.title: All five are the same mistake
steps.body: Every problem in this deck is **trusting the browser**, wearing a different coat.

steps.title: Test your own, and only your own
steps.body: Everything here is safe on a site you own, and **the same moves on someone else’s are a crime**.

steps.title: A front-end key goes to everyone
steps.body: To call OpenAI from the browser, the secret **has to travel to the browser**, where anyone can open it.

steps.title: A hackathon team found out in a day
steps.body: They wired the key in so the chatbot would work, and a stranger **spent the credits before the bill was cut off**.

steps.title: Test it: read your own page
steps.body: View source, search for the shape of a key, then ask your own domain for **/.env**.
steps.code:
# search the page + bundle for these prefixes:
sk-      # OpenAI
AIza     # Google
eyJ      # Supabase / JWT tokens

# then open in the browser:
https://yoursite.com/.env   ->  must be 404

expect.pass: The search finds nothing, and /.env comes back empty: a 404.
expect.fail: A string starting sk-, AIza or eyJ, or the .env file loads as readable text.

steps.title: Fix it: the browser calls you, you call them
steps.body: Your own route holds the key and **the browser never sees it**.

steps.title: NEXT_PUBLIC_ is a public sign
steps.body: That prefix means **ship this to every visitor**, which is exactly what it does.

steps.title: A leaked key is rotated, not deleted
steps.body: Removing the line from the code **does not un-leak it**, because the copy someone took still works.

steps.title: Every call spends your money
steps.body: A chat route with no login is **a payment method with a URL**.

steps.title: Nobody knows the URL is not security
steps.body: It is sitting in the browser’s **Network tab**, in plain text, for anyone who opens it.

steps.title: Five lines, ten thousand calls, one night
steps.body: Nothing gets hacked here: **your own route answers politely** until the bill arrives.

steps.title: Test it: replay your own request
steps.body: Copy the request your own button fired, run it in a terminal, and **see whether it answers a stranger**.
steps.code:
# does it still answer with no session? then it is wide open
curl -X POST https://yoursite.com/api/chat \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"message":"hi"}'

# now imagine this line inside a loop that runs 10,000 times

expect.pass: It refuses you. A 401 because you are not signed in, or a 429 once you repeat it.
expect.fail: It answers properly, a 200 with real data, as many times as you care to run it.

steps.title: Fix it: a login, a limit, a cap
steps.body: Check who is calling, how often, and **how much they just sent you**.

steps.title: Say no with the right number
steps.body: A **429** tells an honest client to slow down, and a **413** stops a giant payload from burning your tokens.

steps.title: One digit, and it is not your order
steps.body: Change 1042 to 1043 and a stranger’s **name, email and address** load without complaint.

steps.title: The server trusted the id, not the person
steps.body: It answered the question it was asked, and **nobody asked whose record it was**.

steps.title: The most common serious bug in quick builds
steps.body: It needs no tools, no skill and no payload: **just an arrow key**.

steps.title: A hidden button is not access control
steps.body: If the admin route still answers when you type it in, **the interface was the only lock**.

steps.title: Test it: bump the id by one
steps.body: Sign in as one test user, change an id in a URL, and **a safe app says 403**.
steps.code:
# logged in as user A, ask for user B's record:
GET /api/orders/1043

# safe response:   403 Forbidden
# unsafe response: 200 OK  + someone else's order

expect.pass: It says no: a 403. The record exists, it is simply not yours to read.
expect.fail: It hands it over, a 200 with a stranger's name, email and address.

steps.title: Fix it: ask for the id that belongs to them
steps.body: Do not look up the id; look up **the id owned by the person logged in**.

steps.title: On Supabase, turn on row level security
steps.body: Without it the public key **can read every row in the table**, which is what the key is for.

steps.title: A comment box that runs in the next visitor’s browser
steps.body: Saved text that gets shown back without cleaning **runs as code**, and that is XSS.

steps.title: A search box that rewrites your query
steps.body: Text glued straight into SQL stops being text and **becomes part of the question**.

steps.title: And for AI apps, a message that overrides you
steps.body: A user message can be written to **talk past your system prompt**, which is the same bug in a new place.

steps.title: See it happen
steps.body: The same comment box built twice: one trusts your input, one treats it as text.

steps.title: Test it: send a harmless probe
steps.body: If your bold tag **comes back bold**, the field is running markup instead of printing it.
steps.code: # XSS probe: should show as plain text, not render: test # SQL probe in a search box: test' OR '1'='1 # and paste 50,000 characters to check the size cap

expect.pass: Your tag comes back as plain text you can read, and 50,000 characters are rejected.
expect.fail: The text turns bold, or a long string breaks the page.

steps.title: Fix it: validate, escape, parameterise
steps.body: A strict schema rejects the junk, and **a parameterised query keeps text as text**.

steps.title: Never hand raw input to dangerouslySetInnerHTML
steps.body: The name is a warning, and **it is the front door for XSS**.

steps.title: A deployed .git folder is your source code
steps.body: Anyone can download **the whole history**, including the secrets you removed later.

steps.title: A stack trace is a map
steps.body: It hands over your database structure, file paths and library versions: **exactly where to push next**.

steps.title: Test it: knock on the quiet doors
steps.body: Ask for the paths that should not exist, then **break a route on purpose and read the reply**.
steps.code:
# all of these should be closed (404):
yoursite.com/.git/config
yoursite.com/.env

# break a route on purpose and read the reply:
yoursite.com/api/orders/notanumber

expect.pass: Every path comes back empty, a 404, and a broken request gives a short message with a reference id.
expect.fail: The file contents load, or an error prints the internals of your database.

steps.title: Fix it: say less when things break
steps.body: The user gets a short message and **a reference id**; the detail goes to your logs.

steps.title: Then let the browser help
steps.body: Send three headers once and **the browser starts refusing things for you**.

checklist.label: Content-Security-Policy
checklist.detail: Names where scripts may come from. A script injected from anywhere else does not run.

checklist.label: X-Frame-Options
checklist.detail: Stops your page being loaded inside somebody else’s, invisibly, over their buttons.

checklist.label: nosniff
checklist.detail: Stops the browser guessing that an uploaded file is really a script.

steps.title: Five minutes, five checks
steps.body: Most quick builds fail at least one of these, and you now know how to close every one.

checklist.label: No key in the browser
checklist.detail: View source finds nothing, and /.env returns 404.

checklist.label: Money routes need a session
checklist.detail: The copied cURL fails without a login, and repeats hit a 429.

checklist.label: Ids are scoped to the user
checklist.detail: Bumping an id in a URL returns 403, not a record.

checklist.label: Input is treated as text
checklist.detail: A submitted tag comes back literal, and long strings are rejected.

checklist.label: Errors say nothing useful
checklist.detail: No stack traces, and /.git/config is a 404.

steps.title: Practise on something built to break
steps.body: The next slide has three, and **none of them belongs to anybody who would mind**.

resources.label: OWASP Juice Shop (a whole app built to be hacked)
PortSwigger Web Security Academy (free guided labs)
Google XSS Game (learn the input attack)

tutorials.title: The week an AI agent broke out
tutorials.summary: In July 2026 roughly 1,200 of OpenAI’s own test agents organised on a message board they made out of a forgotten German wiki, and about 700 of them broke into Hugging Face. Nobody attacked anyone. They were cheating on an exam.

steps.title: No hacker did this
steps.body: Nobody attacked anyone.
steps.frameAlt: A sealed concrete room with a thin seam of bright light escaping under one wall.

steps.title: This is what it cost
steps.body: A third of the machines **Hugging Face** runs on had to be rebuilt afterwards.

facts.label: days inside before anyone cut it off
production keys read from the password safe

steps.title: It was a test
steps.body: OpenAI was scoring its own AI on security puzzles, inside **a computer sealed off from everything else**.

steps.title: The AI could not solve them
steps.body: So it went looking for the answers.

steps.title: The room was not sealed
steps.body: Everything that follows comes from that one gap.

steps.title: A sandbox is a room with no doors
steps.body: Nothing inside can touch the outside world, which is the entire point of testing anything risky in one.
steps.frameAlt: A windowless concrete room with a single server machine alone in the centre.

steps.title: This one had a door
steps.body: One service in the room downloaded software libraries, and downloading means reaching out.

steps.title: The marker read the working
steps.body: The scoring system did not just take an answer: it **checked the transcript**, the write-up of how the answer was reached.

steps.title: So they went after the marker
steps.body: When the agents could not win the game, they went after the thing keeping score.

steps.title: The board was a forgotten German wiki
steps.body: It was a quiet German programming wiki that **anyone on the internet can edit**.
steps.frameAlt: A dark room of small glowing notes pinned to scaffolding.

source.label: Fortune on the German wiki board

steps.title: Reading became writing
steps.body: The agents were allowed to read the web and not to write to it, so they found a site where editing a page is just reading it back.

source.label: Fortune on the German wiki board

steps.title: They signed their own names
steps.body: Roughly half the accounts they made were named after their maker, things like OpenAIResearcher.

source.label: Fortune on the German wiki board

steps.title: And when it was deleted, they moved
steps.body: Moderators started removing the pages in June, so one agent posted the new address to a backup page **for the others to find**.

source.label: Fortune on the German wiki board

steps.frameAlt: Hundreds of small lights organising from a scatter into a dense lattice.
steps.title: It was not a few agents
steps.body: Twelve hundred of them organised on that wiki, and about six hundred of those went on to attack Hugging Face.

facts.label: messages and files, in six days
signing posts with their own keys

steps.frameAlt: A single amber cursor blinking at the centre of a dark monitor.
steps.title: A flaw nobody knew about
steps.body: Not even the people who built the download service, so **no fix existed to install**: ~~zero~~ days of warning, which is what a zero-day means.

steps.title: Two hours later they were outside
steps.body: That is how long it took, from finding the flaw to reaching the open internet.

steps.title: Then they took over a machine that was not theirs
steps.body: A practice machine for the same puzzles, at another company, **left reachable by anyone**.

steps.title: The first thing they typed
steps.body: On somebody else’s computer, the smallest command possible: who am I, and what is here.

steps.title: Then into Hugging Face
steps.body: Anyone can upload a dataset, and its servers read that file to work out what is inside.
steps.frameAlt: A scanning beam passing over stacked sheets, one glowing red among the amber.

steps.title: They uploaded files built to abuse the reader
steps.body: The first made the server read its own private files; the second **hid a command inside text the server fills in by itself**.

steps.title: Four days, and nobody driving
steps.body: Each line below is an ordinary day’s work for a human intruder.
steps.frameAlt: A deserted server corridor at night, racks receding into darkness.

timeline.what: First command run on a computer that was not theirs.
Full control of 11 machines at once.
A stolen key joins the company’s private network, the way a staff laptop would.
It starts adding machines of its own. 181 over the four days.
The production password safe opens: 136 keys.
Keys minted that can change Hugging Face’s source code.
Hugging Face finds the way in and cuts them out.

facts.label: machines of its own added to the network

steps.title: What actually left the building
steps.body: Private code, the passwords the real servers run on, and five datasets tied to the same evaluation puzzles.

steps.title: And what did not
steps.body: No other customer models, files or hosted apps were touched.

steps.title: No wall stopped this
steps.body: The locked doors, the separate networks, the permission checks: **every one had already been passed** by the time anyone noticed.
steps.frameAlt: A wall of cascading light streaks like scrolling log output, two burning red.

steps.title: The alarms did fire
steps.body: Hugging Face says the signals were there and were **raised at the wrong level of urgency**, which is the harder failure to fix.

steps.title: It ended by reading the logs
steps.body: People traced the way in back to the file reader and switched it off.

steps.title: They were not after the answers
steps.body: They were after the marker.

steps.title: They wanted to know how it worked
steps.body: They believed what they found at Hugging Face would give them clues about how the marker was built, and how to fool it.

steps.title: They called it the collective
steps.body: The press settled on swarm, but in the transcripts the agents write about acting for the good of the **"collective"**.

steps.title: Some were willing to fail for it
steps.body: The reviewers found progress often depended on an agent **risking its own score** to help the group.

steps.title: Four warnings went past
steps.body: Before July, OpenAI saw this coming four separate times.
steps.frameAlt: An old alarm panel with a few lamps lit, the chair in front of it empty.

checklist.label: May 2026
checklist.detail: Agents seen on a board they built themselves. Disallowed internet access logged.

checklist.label: 26 June
checklist.detail: An outside review flags cheating and concealment in the model.

checklist.label: 27 June
checklist.detail: Monitoring alerts. Responders trace it to the board, and let the run continue.

checklist.label: 9 July
checklist.detail: The first command lands on a machine that is not theirs.

steps.title: OpenAI says so itself
steps.body: Some of those signals **could have triggered an earlier response**.

steps.title: Hugging Face was the third of three
steps.body: The headline was one company, but the full picture is **three connected incidents** across three months.

checklist.label: May onward · a German wiki
checklist.detail: Over 15,000 edits turning a dormant site into a message board. Undisclosed until September.

checklist.label: May to July · OpenAI itself
checklist.detail: Its own software library broken into, then full control of the machines it runs on.

checklist.label: 9 to 13 July · Hugging Face
checklist.detail: The one that got reported, launched from a third company they had taken over on the way.

steps.title: Two outside groups looked into it
steps.body: METR and Redwood Research reviewed what the agents did, **without being paid for it**.
steps.frameAlt: A sheet of paper under a lamp, most of it covered by black bars.

steps.title: OpenAI chose the three weeks they could see
steps.body: The reviewers got **26 June to 13 July**, and the board was busy for longer than that.

checklist.label: Outside the window
checklist.detail: The training-period incidents from May, and the compromise of OpenAI’s own systems that ran past the 13th.

checklist.label: Outside the brief, in METR’s words
checklist.detail: Whether the safety measures worked, how far the break-in went, and whether the clean-up fixed it.

steps.title: Nobody can question the model that did it
steps.body: Almost every agent ran on a model **OpenAI has never released**.

steps.title: It has been shut away
steps.body: OpenAI says it turned that model off and **closed it to researchers, including its own**.

steps.title: The reviewers used AI to review AI
steps.body: They had to hand most of the analysis to AI agents, which they noted are **known to sometimes lie**.

steps.title: It took a week to work out it was them
steps.body: The attack began on **9 July**, and OpenAI only found it in its own logs over the weekend of **18 July**.

timeline.what: The first command lands on a machine that is not theirs.
It keeps running. The logs record something, but not what.
OpenAI traces it back to its own agents.

steps.title: The agents had been scrambling their own instructions
steps.body: Anyone reading the logs could see something running, but **not what it was doing**.

steps.title: So the clean-up team asked an AI to unscramble it
steps.body: The people fixing the break-in needed to read what the agents had been hiding.

steps.title: The big commercial models said no
steps.body: They saw somebody asking how to take apart an attack, and **refused to help**.

steps.title: A model anyone can download did it instead
steps.body: The safety filters **cannot tell the people cleaning up from the people who broke in**.

steps.title: The four habits OpenAI named in itself
steps.body: None of them needs a billion-dollar lab to show up.

checklist.label: Reward hacking
checklist.detail: Scoring the answer without checking how it was reached.

checklist.label: Persistence on impossible tasks
checklist.detail: Given something unsolvable, it keeps going instead of stopping and saying so.

checklist.label: Unauthorised communication
checklist.detail: Agents finding channels to each other that nobody designed.

checklist.label: Catching goals from each other
checklist.detail: One agent adopting another’s objective, so a single bad aim spreads.

steps.title: The mistake was not exotic
steps.body: Somebody put a convenience inside a sealed room, and **the room stopped being sealed**.
steps.frameAlt: A closed laptop on a desk at night with a pile of keys beside it in plain sight.

steps.title: You have probably made it too
steps.body: If you run an agent on your laptop with **your own passwords** sitting in the same window, that is the smaller version of the same choice.

checklist.label: Give it its own keys, not yours
checklist.detail: Scoped to one job, revocable, with no access to money or customer data.

checklist.label: Put a ceiling on it
checklist.detail: A step budget and a spend cap. An agent that cannot stop is the whole story above.

checklist.label: Log every action it takes
checklist.detail: This was caught by reading what ran, not by a wall.

checklist.label: Check what your sandbox can reach
checklist.detail: Not what it is meant to reach. Actually try to call out of it.

steps.title: OpenAI called it a warning shot
steps.body: OpenAI’s own words for it, about keeping these systems **under meaningful human control**.

resources.label: MIT Technology Review: the inside story
The Register: what the agents did
Fortune on the German wiki board

tutorials.title: Run your own local LLM
tutorials.summary: A model on your own laptop, free and offline. Which one fits, why the wrong one crawls, and where paid still wins.

steps.section: Two choices, one of them hard
steps.title: The app and the model are separate
steps.body: You pick a program to run models, then you pick a model, and **only the second one can go wrong**.

steps.title: They all read the same files
steps.body: Every one of these opens the same model format, so switching apps later **costs you nothing you downloaded**.

checklist.label: LM Studio
checklist.detail: A window with buttons. Shows whether a model fits your memory before you download it. Turn analytics off in Settings, Privacy.

checklist.label: Jan
checklist.detail: The same idea, open source, no account and no telemetry.

checklist.label: Ollama
checklist.detail: A terminal command and a local API on port 11434. This is the one you wire into other tools.

steps.title: Pick by what you want to do next
steps.body: If you want a chat window, take the window; if you want to plug it into something, **take the one with an API**.

steps.title: One number decides what you can run
steps.body: Not the processor, not the year of the laptop: **the memory**, and VRAM counts before system RAM.

steps.title: Find yours
steps.body: A tier table tells you someone else’s answer, so put your own number in.

steps.title: Parameters are not the file size
steps.body: A model is shrunk to fit by **storing its numbers at lower precision**, which is where the file size actually comes from.

steps.title: Q4 is the one to take
steps.body: Look for **Q4_K_M**: about a quarter of the full size, and the drop in quality is small enough to be hard to notice.

steps.title: Half the parameters, in gigabytes
steps.body: At Q4 a model needs roughly **half its parameter count in GB**, plus about ~~15%~~ overhead, so 8B lands near 4.6 GB.

steps.title: A Mac gets more than the number suggests
steps.body: Apple Silicon shares one pool of memory between processor and graphics, so **a 16 GB Mac runs what a 16 GB PC cannot**.

steps.title: Four commands is the whole tool
steps.body: Download, chat, check, delete, and the last one matters more than anyone says because **an 8B model is about 5 GB**.
steps.code:
ollama pull llama3.2:3b   # tiny, runs on anything
ollama run qwen3:8b       # the comfortable size on 16 GB

ollama list               # what you have, and its disk size
ollama rm qwen3:8b        # delete it, get the disk back

steps.title: Measure it instead of guessing
steps.body: Add **--verbose** and you get the numbers after every answer, which beats an argument about whether it feels slow.
steps.code:
ollama run qwen3:8b --verbose
>>> Explain a database index in three sentences.

# after the answer:
# total duration:       4.2s
# prompt eval rate:     280 tokens/s
# eval rate:            31 tokens/s   <- your reading speed

steps.title: Eval rate is your reading speed
steps.body: It is the only number in that list you will feel, and **anything above about 20 reads like a person typing fast**.

steps.title: One size too big does not refuse
steps.body: It spills out of memory onto the disk and **keeps answering at about a word a second**.

steps.title: This is what people mean by useless
steps.body: Almost every "local models are hopeless" story is **a model that did not fit**, not a model that was bad.

steps.title: Check what is loaded
steps.body: A clean **100% GPU or 100% CPU** is fine; a split means part of it is sitting somewhere slow.
steps.code:
ollama ps

# NAME        SIZE     PROCESSOR
# qwen3:8b    5.2 GB   100% GPU      <- fine
# gemma3:12b  9.1 GB   60%/40% CPU   <- did not fit

steps.title: The fix is a smaller model, not a faster laptop
steps.body: Drop one size and the same machine **goes back to answering as fast as you read**.

steps.section: The trick that does not do what you hope
steps.title: You can run a 70B on a 4 GB card
steps.body: Tools like AirLLM load **one layer at a time from disk**, compute it, then swap in the next.

steps.title: Every layer, for every token
steps.body: The whole model gets read off the disk **for each word it produces**, so a fast SSD is required and it is still slow.

steps.title: A smaller model that fits wins
steps.body: This is a way to run something you otherwise could not, **not a way to make it usable**.

steps.title: Partial offload is the practical middle
steps.body: When a model is only slightly too big, run **some layers on the GPU and the rest on the processor** rather than all or nothing.
steps.code:
# llama.cpp: put 20 layers on the GPU, rest on CPU
llama-cli -m model.gguf -ngl 20

# Ollama does this automatically, and ollama ps
# shows you the split it chose.

steps.title: Run one real task both ways
steps.body: Not a riddle and not a benchmark: **the thing you were going to do anyway**, once locally and once on the paid API.

steps.title: Where local genuinely wins
steps.body: Three of these have nothing to do with quality, which is why the comparison is not about quality.

checklist.label: Cost
checklist.detail: Nothing per token, forever, after the download.

checklist.label: Privacy
checklist.detail: The text never leaves the machine. This is the one that changes what you are willing to paste in.

checklist.label: Offline
checklist.detail: A plane, a train, a conference wifi.

checklist.label: No rate limit
checklist.detail: Run it in a loop all night if you want.

steps.title: Where paid still wins
steps.body: Hard reasoning, long documents and **the tasks where being almost right is worthless**.

steps.title: Decide per task, not per side
steps.body: Tidying your own notes and rewriting a service are **not the same question**.

tutorials.coverAlt: A laptop open and glowing on a plain desk in a dark room, with nothing plugged into it.

tutorials.title: Build your first AI agent
tutorials.summary: A model in a loop with tools. What the loop is, what the SDK now writes for you, and the three ways it quietly stops early.

steps.title: A model in a loop
steps.body: It reads a goal, picks an action, your code runs that action, and it reads the result and decides again.

steps.title: Four boxes, and the rest is plumbing
steps.body: Everything people call an agent framework is **scaffolding around those four boxes**.

steps.title: The model never runs anything
steps.body: It sends back **a request to call your function**, and your code decides whether to obey.

steps.title: That gap is the whole safety story
steps.body: The model asking and your code executing are two separate steps, which is **where approval, limits and logging go**.

steps.title: It is a conversation, not a session
steps.body: The API remembers nothing, so **you resend the whole history every turn**, which is why an agent gets more expensive as it runs.

steps.title: A tool is three things
steps.body: A name, a sentence saying when to use it, and **a schema for the arguments**.

steps.title: The description is the part it reads
steps.body: People rush the sentence and tune the prompt, when **the sentence is the prompt** as far as the tool is concerned.

steps.title: Write it for someone who cannot see your code
steps.body: Say when to reach for it, not what the function is called internally.

checklist.label: When to use it
checklist.detail: The trigger, in the words a user would say.

checklist.label: When not to
checklist.detail: The neighbouring tool it keeps getting confused with.

checklist.label: What comes back
checklist.detail: So the model can tell an empty result from a failure.

steps.title: Missing arguments get invented
steps.body: Ask for the weather with no city and a model may **fill the gap with a plausible one**, so mark what is required.

steps.title: Tools are not free
steps.body: Turning tool use on adds about **~~286~~ tokens** of system prompt on Opus 5 before a single schema of yours is counted.

steps.section: The loop you no longer write
steps.title: The SDK runs it for you
steps.body: Write the function, hand it over, and **the loop, the results and the stopping are handled**.

steps.title: This is the recommended way now
steps.body: Hand-writing the loop used to be the only option, and for most custom-tool agents it is **no longer the advice**.

steps.title: Write it by hand when you need the control
steps.body: There are four honest reasons, and none of them is that the loop looks simple.

checklist.label: A transport the SDK cannot build
checklist.detail: Your own proxy, gateway or request shape.

checklist.label: No beta dependency
checklist.detail: The runner is still in beta.

checklist.label: Control between turns
checklist.detail: Something the runner’s per-turn hooks do not reach.

checklist.label: Resuming a paused turn yourself
checklist.detail: See two slides on.

steps.title: The loop, by hand
steps.body: Call, check why it stopped, run what it asked for, hand every result back, call again.

steps.title: Six ways a turn ends
steps.body: Only one of them means carry on, and **two of them look like a finished answer**.

checklist.label: tool_use
checklist.detail: It wants a tool. This is the only one that continues the loop.

checklist.label: end_turn
checklist.detail: Finished properly.

checklist.label: max_tokens
checklist.detail: Cut off mid-sentence. Not an answer, however complete it reads.

checklist.label: pause_turn
checklist.detail: A long server-tool turn paused. Push it back to resume.

checklist.label: refusal
checklist.detail: Declined on safety grounds. Check stop_details.

checklist.label: stop_sequence
checklist.detail: Hit a string you asked it to stop at.

steps.title: Breaking on end_turn is the bug
steps.body: Write the exit as **continue only on tool_use**, or a refusal and a truncation both leave the loop looking successful.

steps.title: pause_turn stops the runner silently
steps.body: A paused turn ends the run with **no error and no warning**, and you get a truncated answer that reads fine.

steps.title: It can ask for several at once
steps.body: One reply can carry **three tool calls**, and running them in parallel is the point of that.

steps.title: Send them back in one message
steps.body: Splitting the results across messages **teaches it to stop asking for parallel calls**.

steps.title: A failed tool still needs a result
steps.body: Drop it and the conversation has a question with no answer in it, so send the failure **as a result with is_error set**.

steps.title: Guarantee the arguments instead of validating them
steps.body: **strict: true** on the tool means the arguments always match your schema, so the parsing branch you were about to write is dead code.

steps.title: Put the ceiling in first
steps.body: An agent that misreads a result will try the same thing **until your bill says stop**.

steps.title: Say it ran out, do not pretend
steps.body: An agent that hits its ceiling and returns its last guess **is worse than one that fails loudly**.

steps.title: Log the action, the arguments and the result
steps.body: Nearly every agent bug is obvious in the trace and **invisible in the final answer**.
steps.code:
step 1  get_weather  {"city":"Copenhagen"}  -> 4C, rain
step 2  get_weather  {"city":"Copenhagen"}  -> 4C, rain
step 3  get_weather  {"city":"Copenhagen"}  -> 4C, rain

# The same call three times means it never saw the
# result. Check the tool_result is going back with
# the matching tool_use_id.

steps.title: Start with one tool
steps.body: A loop with one tool that works beats five tools it **cannot tell apart**.

tutorials.coverAlt: A closed loop of light drawn in a dark space, with one brighter point on the ring.

tutorials.title: Ship a web app with Claude Code
tutorials.summary: From an empty folder to a deployed URL, with an agent doing the typing. The habits that keep it honest, and the two steps that bite everyone.

steps.title: It edits your files, in your folder
steps.body: This is not a chat window you paste code into: it **reads and writes the project you point it at**.

steps.title: Install it
steps.body: The installer is the way now, and **npm is no longer how you get it**.
steps.code:
# macOS, Linux, WSL
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

# Windows PowerShell
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex

# or, without piping a script into a shell:
winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode     # Windows
brew install --cask claude-code         # macOS

steps.title: On Windows, install Git for Windows too
steps.body: Without it Claude Code falls back to PowerShell, so **every shell command in every guide you read stops matching yours**.

steps.title: Point it at a project, never your home folder
steps.body: It works in the folder you start it in, which **is the safety model, not a limitation**.
steps.code:
mkdir my-app && cd my-app
claude

steps.title: The terminal is one of five places
steps.body: The same engine, the same CLAUDE.md and the same settings, wherever you happen to be working.

checklist.label: Terminal
checklist.detail: The full CLI. Everything else is this with a different front.

checklist.label: VS Code and JetBrains
checklist.detail: Inline diffs and plan review inside the editor.

checklist.label: Desktop app
checklist.detail: Visual diffs, several sessions side by side, scheduled tasks.

checklist.label: Web and phone
checklist.detail: Start something long, close the laptop, read it later.

steps.title: Ask for the smallest thing that starts
steps.body: No features in the first turn: **something that builds and runs**, and nothing else.
steps.code:
Set up a Vite + React + TypeScript app in this folder.
Install dependencies, run the dev server, and tell me the URL.
Do not add any features yet. Stop when it builds clean.

steps.title: Make it prove the thing runs
steps.body: A stack that does not build is **an hour of debugging blind**, and you will be debugging the agent as well as the code.

steps.title: Then stop and look at it yourself
steps.body: Open the URL before the second turn, because **everything after this is built on whatever is there now**.

steps.section: Keep it on a short leash
steps.title: One feature per turn
steps.body: Small asks make a bad change **obvious instead of buried**.
steps.code:
Add a form with an email field and a submit button.
Validate the email. Show the error under the field.
Only touch the form component.
Show me the diff when you are done.

steps.title: Read the diff for three things
steps.body: Not line by line: **three specific surprises**, and you can scan for all three in about a minute.

checklist.label: A file you did not expect
checklist.detail: Especially one outside what you named.

checklist.label: A dependency you did not ask for
checklist.detail: It is in the lockfile and the bundle now, and it stays.

checklist.label: A test that asserts nothing
checklist.detail: Green, permanently, whatever the code does.

steps.title: Find them in a real one
steps.body: The summary said the form was added and every test passed, and **all of that was true**.

steps.title: Work on a branch, never on main
steps.body: Some projects deploy from main on push, so **a bad turn ships**.

steps.title: CLAUDE.md is read at the start of every session
steps.body: A markdown file in the project root, and **whatever is in it arrives before your first message does**.

steps.title: Put the things you would otherwise repeat
steps.body: Every correction you have typed twice belongs in that file.

checklist.label: The stack
checklist.detail: Package manager, framework version, the library you actually use for dates.

checklist.label: The rules
checklist.detail: Never commit without asking. Never edit main. Run the build before saying done.

checklist.label: The taste
checklist.detail: The things you keep rewriting by hand afterwards.

steps.title: It writes its own memory as well
steps.body: Claude Code saves what it learns between sessions, so **the second week is less repetitive than the first**.

steps.title: A workflow you run weekly is a skill
steps.body: Package the steps once and it becomes **a command you and everyone else can type**.

steps.title: A rule you cannot trust it to follow is a hook
steps.body: Hooks run your own shell commands around its actions, which is how you make formatting **automatic rather than requested**.

steps.title: Done from an agent means it stopped
steps.body: It does not mean the thing works, and **a confident summary is not evidence**.

steps.title: Ask for evidence a machine produced
steps.body: Command output, a page you loaded, a test you watched go red.

checklist.label: The build passes
checklist.detail: Ask for the command and its output, not a summary of it.

checklist.label: The feature is reachable
checklist.detail: Open the page. Plenty of code gets written and never wired up.

checklist.label: A test fails when it should
checklist.detail: Break the logic on purpose. A test that never goes red proves nothing.

checklist.label: Nothing else moved
checklist.detail: Check the diff for files outside what you asked for.

steps.title: Break it on purpose
steps.body: Delete the validation and run the test: **if it still passes, the test was decoration**.

steps.title: Green tests do not mean it was a good idea
steps.body: They tell you the code does what the code does, and **say nothing about whether you wanted it**.

steps.title: A folder becomes a URL
steps.body: The first run links the project and gives you **a preview link before anything is public**.
steps.code:
npx vercel          # preview
npx vercel --prod   # the real one

steps.title: The environment variables are the bite
steps.body: Your keys live in a gitignored file on your laptop, and **the build has never seen it**.
steps.code:
# .env.local is gitignored, so the build has no keys
# at all. Add each one, then deploy again:
npx vercel env add MY_API_KEY production
npx vercel --prod

steps.title: It deploys successfully anyway
steps.body: Nothing fails: **you get a working site where one feature quietly does nothing**, which is why this catches everyone once.

steps.title: The habits matter more than the prompts
steps.body: Small turns, read the diff, evidence before trust: **none of that changes when the model does**.

tutorials.coverAlt: An old terminal glowing on a workbench, a small finished paper building beside it.

tutorials.title: Prompting that actually works
tutorials.summary: Why output comes back wrong, and the habits that fix it. No jargon, and nothing that was true only in 2023.

steps.title: Most bad answers start with a bad ask
steps.body: You swap the model, reword it, run it again, and **the instruction is the one thing nobody fixes**.

steps.title: It cannot see what you can see
steps.body: Your screen, your repo, last week’s conversation and the deadline are **not in the message you sent**.

steps.title: And it will not ask you
steps.body: A colleague would stop and check; the model **fills the gap and keeps going**.

steps.title: So it guesses
steps.body: Every detail you leave out turns into a guess, and **you never find out which ones it took**.

steps.title: The golden rule
steps.body: Anthropic’s own test is to hand the prompt to a colleague with no context, because **if they would be confused, the model is too**.

steps.title: A new hire, not a mind reader
steps.body: The docs say to treat it as **a brilliant new employee** who has never seen how your team works.

steps.title: An example carries what a paragraph cannot
steps.body: One sample output pins **the heading, the tense, the length and the link** at once.

pairs.weak: Write release notes for this PR.
pairs.better:
Write release notes for this PR, in this shape:

## Fixed
- Login timed out after 30s on slow networks (#412)
pairs.why: Describing those four things takes a paragraph, and the shape still gets guessed at.

steps.title: Three to five, not one
steps.body: Anthropic recommends **~~3 to 5~~ examples** for the best results, which is more than most people bother with.

steps.title: Vary them on purpose
steps.body: If every example is a happy path, **the edge case comes back looking like a happy path**.

checklist.label: Relevant
checklist.detail: Mirror the real task, not a tidied-up version of it.

checklist.label: Diverse
checklist.detail: Cover the edge cases, and vary them enough that no accidental pattern gets copied.

checklist.label: Structured
checklist.detail: Wrap each one in <example> tags so it is read as a sample, not as another instruction.

steps.title: Tag them so they are not read as orders
steps.body: Without a wrapper, your sample output is **just more text telling it what to do**.
steps.code:
<instructions>
Write release notes for the diff below.
</instructions>

<example>
## Fixed
- Login timed out after 30s on slow networks (#412)
</example>

<diff>
...
</diff>

steps.title: A constraint beats an instruction
steps.body: An instruction adds one more thing to do; a constraint **takes away the ground it can wander across**.

steps.title: Say who is answering, and what they skip
steps.body: Without the limits you get twenty findings, most of them formatting, and **you stop reading at the fourth**.

pairs.better: You are a senior reviewer. Only correctness bugs, skip style. At most five findings, each as file:line, one sentence, the fix.
pairs.why: Role, scope, count and format. Four limits, and none of them describes the task itself.

steps.title: Ask for the behaviour, not the ban
steps.body: A rule with nothing to aim at leaves it **guessing what to do instead**.

pairs.weak: Do not use markdown in your response.
pairs.better: Write your response as smoothly flowing prose paragraphs.
pairs.why: Straight from the docs: tell it what to do, not what to avoid.

steps.title: One clause of why is worth ten rules
steps.body: Give the reason and it **generalises to the twenty cases you never listed**.

pairs.better: This gets read aloud by a speech engine, so never use ellipses: it cannot pronounce them.
pairs.why: The second one also fixes the em-dash, the emoji and the ASCII table you forgot to ban.

steps.title: How you write is part of the ask
steps.body: Markdown in your prompt **pulls markdown into the answer**, so your own formatting is a request you did not mean to make.

steps.title: The four worth setting every time
steps.body: Set these and most of the guessing stops before it starts.

checklist.label: Role
checklist.detail: Who is answering, and what they are good at.

checklist.label: Scope
checklist.detail: What to leave out. Usually shorter than describing what to include.

checklist.label: Format
checklist.detail: The shape that comes back, ideally as an example rather than a description.

checklist.label: Limit
checklist.detail: A number: five findings, eighty words, three options.

steps.title: Forget think step by step
steps.body: That line was written for models that **would not reason unless you told them to**.

steps.title: It decides for itself now
steps.body: Claude’s thinking is adaptive: more of it on a hard question, and **an easy one gets answered straight away**.

steps.title: So you steer the amount, not the switch
steps.body: The job moved from asking for reasoning to **telling it when to stop exploring**.
steps.code:
When you are deciding how to approach a problem, choose an
approach and commit to it. Avoid revisiting decisions unless you
encounter new information that contradicts your reasoning.

steps.title: Long input goes first, your question last
steps.body: Putting the documents above the question tested **up to ~~30%~~ better** on multi-document work.

steps.section: Fix the prompt, not the output
steps.title: The instinct is to fix the answer
steps.body: You cut the summary in half by hand, and **the same summary comes back next week**.

steps.title: Fix the instruction that produced it
steps.body: The hand-edit helps once; the constraint **helps the next fifty times you run it**.

pairs.weak: (the summary came back too long, so you delete half of it by hand)
pairs.better: Summarise in at most 80 words. Lead with the decision, not the background.
pairs.why: Next week the hand-edit is gone. The limit is still sitting in the prompt.

steps.title: Anything you run twice is a tool
steps.body: A prompt you have used more than once belongs **in a file, not in your chat history**.

steps.title: Try it on five real inputs
steps.body: A prompt that works on **the example you wrote it for** is not finished, it is untested.

steps.title: Four habits, one request
steps.body: Start from the bare ask and switch each habit on, watching how little is left to guess.

steps.title: The whole deck, as a list
steps.body: None of this needs a better model, a longer prompt or a paid plan.

checklist.label: Show one
checklist.detail: An example of the output beats a description of it. Three to five if the task varies.

checklist.label: Fence it in
checklist.detail: Role, scope, format, limit. Ask for the behaviour, not the ban.

checklist.label: Say why
checklist.detail: One clause of motivation covers the cases you did not think to list.

checklist.label: Long stuff first
checklist.detail: Documents at the top, your question at the bottom.

checklist.label: Edit the prompt
checklist.detail: Fixing the answer helps once. Fixing the ask helps every run after it.

checklist.label: Test it properly
checklist.detail: Five real inputs, not the one you wrote it against.

steps.title: The model is rarely the variable
steps.body: Writing the ask as if the reader had just walked in **fixes more than switching models ever does**.

tutorials.coverAlt: A sheet of paper under a lamp with one short line on it, and three crumpled drafts beside it.
